{{no footnotes|date=September 2018}}
In mathematics, the '''Duflo isomorphism''' is an [[isomorphism]] between the center of the [[universal enveloping algebra]] of a finite-dimensional [[Lie algebra]] over a [[Characteristic_0#Fields_of_characteristic_zero|field of characteristic zero]] and the invariants of its [[symmetric algebra]]. It was introduced by {{harvs|txt|first=Michel|last=Duflo|author-link=Michel Duflo|year=1977}} and  later generalized to arbitrary finite-dimensional Lie algebras by [[Maxim Kontsevich]].

The [[Poincaré–Birkhoff–Witt_theorem|Poincaré-Birkoff-Witt theorem]] gives for any Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> a vector space isomorphism from the polynomial algebra <math>S(\mathfrak{g})</math> to the universal enveloping algebra <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math>.   This map is not an algebra homomorphism.    It is equivariant with respect to the natural representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> on these spaces, so it restricts to a vector space isomorphism
: <math>F\colon S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} \to  U(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} </math>
where the superscript indicates the subspace annihilated by the action of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.   Both <math>S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}}</math> and <math>U(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}}</math> are commutative subalgebras, indeed <math>U(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}}</math> is the center of <math>U(\mathfrak{g})</math>, but <math>F</math> is still not an algebra homomorphism.  However, Duflo proved that in some cases we can compose <math>F</math> with a map 
: <math>G \colon S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} \to  S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} </math>
to get an algebra isomorphism
:<math>  F \circ G \colon S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} \to  U(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} .</math>
Later, using the [[Kontsevich formality theorem]], Kontsevich showed that this works for all finite-dimensional Lie algebras.  

Following Calaque and Rossi, the map <math>G</math> can be defined as follows.  The [[adjoint action]] of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is the map
: <math> \mathfrak{g} \to \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g}) </math>
sending <math>x \in \mathfrak{g}</math> to the operation <math>[x,-]</math> on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.   We can treat map as an element of
: <math>  \mathfrak{g}^\ast \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math>
or, for that matter, an element of the larger space <math>S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math>, since <math> \mathfrak{g}^\ast \subset S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast)</math>.  Call this element
: <math> \mathrm{ad} \in S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math>
Both <math>S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast)</math> and <math>\mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math> are algebras so their tensor product is as well.  Thus, we can take powers of <math>\mathrm{ad}</math>, say
: <math> \mathrm{ad}^k \in S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g}).</math>
Going further, we can apply any [[formal power series]] to <math>\mathrm{ad}</math> and obtain an element of <math>\overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math>, where <math>\overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast)</math> denotes the algebra of formal [[power series]] on <math>\mathfrak{g}^\ast</math>.   Working with formal power series and applying the hypothesis that <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> is defined over a field of characteristic zero, we thus obtain an element
: <math> \sqrt{\frac{e^{\mathrm{ad}/2} - e^{-\mathrm{ad}/2}}{\mathrm{ad}}} \in \overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g}) </math>
Since the dimension of <math>  \mathfrak{g} </math> is finite, one can think of <math> \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g})</math> as <math> \mathrm{M}_n(\mathbb{R})</math>, hence <math> \overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) \otimes \mathrm{End}(\mathfrak{g}) </math> is <math> \mathrm{M}_n(\overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast)) </math> and by applying the determinant map, we obtain an element
: <math> \tilde{J}^{1/2} := \mathrm{det} \sqrt{\frac{e^{\mathrm{ad}/2} - e^{-\mathrm{ad}/2}}{\mathrm{ad}}} \in \overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) </math><ref>Calaque 2011, p. 4 (Remark 1.4).</ref>
which is related to the [[Todd class]] in algebraic topology.

Now, <math>\mathfrak{g}^\ast</math> acts as derivations on <math>S(\mathfrak{g})</math> since any element of <math>\mathfrak{g}^\ast</math> gives a translation-invariant vector field on <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>.   As a result, the algebra <math>S(\mathfrak{g}^\ast) </math> acts on 
as differential operators on <math>S(\mathfrak{g})</math>, and this extends to an action of <math>\overline{S}(\mathfrak{g}^\ast)</math> on <math>S(\mathfrak{g})</math>.   We can thus define a linear map
: <math>G \colon S(\mathfrak{g}) \to S(\mathfrak{g}) </math>
by
: <math> G(\psi) = \tilde{J}^{1/2} \psi </math>
and since the whole construction was invariant, <math>G</math> restricts to the desired linear map
: <math>G \colon S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} \to  S(\mathfrak{g})^{\mathfrak{g}} .</math>

==Properties==
For a [[nilpotent Lie algebra]] the Duflo isomorphism coincides with the symmetrization map from [[symmetric algebra]] to [[universal enveloping algebra]]. For a [[semisimple Lie algebra]] the Duflo isomorphism is  compatible in a natural way with the [[Harish-Chandra isomorphism]].
